trig-waves-phase-sinusoidal-mathematical.title: Sinusoidal mathematical models
trig-waves-phase-sinusoidal-mathematical.summary: Interpret a sinusoidal function as a model of a periodic quantity, including its amplitude, midpoint, angular rate and initial phase.

blocks.text: A sinusoidal model is y(t)=D+A sin(ωt+φ), or a cosine model. Its midline is D, its amplitude is |A|, and for nonzero ω the period is 2π/|ω|. A negative A reflects the waveform about its midline. For nonzero A, the range is [D−|A|,D+|A|]. State the input units and angle mode before evaluating.

blocks.caption: Original schematic for sinusoidal mathematical models; waveforms use idealized quantities and labeled reference conventions, with exact computations in the lesson formulas.

blocks.title: Read a sinusoidal model
blocks.problem: For y=2+3sin(4πt), identify the amplitude, mean and period.
blocks.strategy: Read A, D and ω from the standard form.
steps: The period is 2π/(4π)=0.5 time units; the range is [−1,5].
blocks.check: Substitute sin=1 and sin=−1 to check both endpoints.

blocks.title: Interpret a reflected cosine
blocks.problem: For y=1−2cos(πt), find the maximum and minimum.
blocks.strategy: Use cos(πt)∈[−1,1] and track the minus sign.
steps: The amplitude is |−2|=2, and the midline is 1.
The maximum is 1−2(−1)=3 and the minimum is 1−2(1)=−1.
blocks.check: Direct substitution at t=1 and t=0 confirms the extrema.

sections.title: Common mistakes, checkpoint, and reference guide

blocks.text: Amplitude is never negative; A may be negative. Do not confuse the midpoint D with the amplitude or assume ω itself is the frequency in hertz.

blocks.prompt: What is the range of 4−2sin t?
blocks.explanation: Since sin t ranges from −1 to 1, the range is 4±2, namely 2 through 6.

blocks.text: Reference guide (original lessons and questions): Lial 10th ed. §§4.1–4.2; Sullivan 9th ed. §2.6; Young 3rd ed. Chapter 4. Verify wave and phasor sign conventions before applying results.

trig-waves-phase-amplitude-period-freque.title: Amplitude, period, frequency, and angular frequency
trig-waves-phase-amplitude-period-freque.summary: Convert accurately among period, ordinary frequency, angular frequency, radians and cycles for sinusoidal signals.

blocks.text: One complete cycle corresponds to 2π radians. Frequency f counts cycles each second (hertz); period T measures seconds per cycle; angular frequency ω measures radians per second. These formulas assume a nonconstant oscillatory signal and consistent time units. In y=sin(bt), the angular frequency is |b| when t is in seconds.

blocks.caption: Original schematic for amplitude, period, frequency, and angular frequency; waveforms use idealized quantities and labeled reference conventions, with exact computations in the lesson formulas.

blocks.title: Power-line frequency
blocks.problem: Find T and ω for a 50 Hz sinusoidal signal.
blocks.strategy: Use the reciprocal-frequency and radians-per-cycle relationships.
blocks.check: A complete 100π·0.02=2π-radian phase change occurs in one period.

blocks.title: Read a sine coefficient
blocks.problem: Find the frequency and period of y=sin(12πt).
blocks.strategy: The coefficient of t is angular frequency in rad/s.
blocks.check: 6 cycles per second gives approximately 0.1667 s per cycle.

sections.title: Common mistakes, checkpoint, and reference guide

blocks.text: Hertz and rad/s are not interchangeable: ω=2πf, not ω=f. For example, a frequency of 60 Hz means 120π rad/s.

blocks.explanation: Convert 4 ms to 0.004 s, then calculate f=1/0.004=250 Hz.

blocks.text: Reference guide (original lessons and questions): Lial 10th ed. §3.4 and §4.1; Schaum’s 4th ed. §§1.7 and 7.5; Sullivan 9th ed. §2.6. Verify wave and phasor sign conventions before applying results.

trig-waves-phase-phase-shift-versus-time.title: Phase shift versus time shift
trig-waves-phase-phase-shift-versus-time.summary: Relate phase angle in radians or degrees to horizontal graph shift and physical time advance or delay with a fixed angular rate.

blocks.text: In y(t)=A sin(ωt+φ), an initial phase φ moves the same sinusoid along the time axis. For positive ω, positive φ is an advance (left shift) of φ/ω seconds, while negative φ is a delay (right shift) of |φ|/ω. A time delay t₀ produces sin(ω(t−t₀)) and hence phase −ωt₀. Always use radians with ω in rad/s.

blocks.caption: Original schematic for phase shift versus time shift; waveforms use idealized quantities and labeled reference conventions, with exact computations in the lesson formulas.

blocks.title: Time delay from phase
blocks.problem: For sin(100πt−π/2), compute the time delay relative to sin(100πt).
blocks.strategy: Use ω=100π rad/s and the negative phase shift.
steps: The phase is −π/2 radians, giving delay t₀=(π/2)/(100π).
t₀=1/200 s=5 ms to the right.

blocks.title: Advance from a positive phase
blocks.problem: For sin(20t+π/5), calculate the time advance.
blocks.strategy: Divide positive phase in radians by positive ω.
steps: The phase is +π/5 and ω=20 rad/s.
blocks.check: Replacing t by t+π/100 reproduces the original argument.

sections.title: Common mistakes, checkpoint, and reference guide

blocks.text: The graph phase angle φ and time shift −φ/ω have opposite signs for ω>0. Do not mix degrees into a calculation using rad/s without converting.

blocks.prompt: Does sin(10t−2) advance or lag sin(10t), and by how much?
blocks.explanation: The negative phase −2 rad at ω=10 rad/s corresponds to a shift of +2/10=0.2 s.

blocks.text: Reference guide (original lessons and questions): Sullivan 9th ed. §2.6; Lial 10th ed. §4.2; Young 3rd ed. Chapter 4. Verify wave and phasor sign conventions before applying results.

trig-waves-phase-phase-difference-and-le.title: Phase difference and lead–lag relationships
trig-waves-phase-phase-difference-and-le.summary: Determine which of two equal-frequency sinusoids leads or lags and convert phase differences to time separations.

blocks.text: For two sinusoids of equal positive angular frequency ω, compare the phase terms using the same reference function (both sine or both cosine). A larger phase is earlier in time and leads; a smaller phase lags. Phase is defined modulo 2π, so name an interval such as (−π,π] when giving a signed shortest phase difference. Use Δt=|Δφ|/ω to convert angular separation into time.

blocks.caption: Original schematic for phase difference and lead–lag relationships; waveforms use idealized quantities and labeled reference conventions, with exact computations in the lesson formulas.

blocks.title: Determine the leading waveform
blocks.strategy: Both are sine signals at the same frequency, so subtract their phases.
steps: Voltage v leads current i by 90° (or current lags by 90°).
blocks.check: At an increasing zero crossing, the signal with the greater phase crosses first.

blocks.title: Phase and time separation
blocks.problem: A pair of 60 Hz sinusoids are separated by 120°. Find the shorter time offset.
blocks.strategy: A 120° phase separation is one third of a full cycle.

sections.title: Common mistakes, checkpoint, and reference guide

blocks.text: Lead/lag comparison requires a common time reference, angular frequency, and sine/cosine convention. Difference greater than 180° should be interpreted with a specified wrapped-phase convention.

blocks.prompt: Relative to sin(ωt), does cos(ωt) lead or lag?
blocks.explanation: cos(ωt)=sin(ωt+π/2), so its phase is 90° greater in the sine reference.

blocks.text: Reference guide (original lessons and questions): Gibilisco, Trigonometry DeMYSTiFieD, Chapter 9; Sullivan 9th ed. §4.5; Lial 10th ed. §4.2. Verify wave and phasor sign conventions before applying results.

trig-waves-phase-combining-same-frequenc.title: Combining same-frequency sinusoids
trig-waves-phase-combining-same-frequenc.summary: Combine same-frequency sine and cosine signals using phase-shift identities or vector addition while preserving amplitudes and signs.

blocks.text: Two sinusoids at the same angular frequency add to a single sinusoid (or zero). Write a sin(ωt)+b cos(ωt)=R sin(ωt+φ), where R=√(a²+b²)≥0 and φ=atan2(b,a). This quadrant-aware phase rule avoids ambiguous inverse tangents. Sinusoids of different frequencies generally cannot be reduced to one simple sinusoid by this method.

blocks.caption: Original schematic for combining same-frequency sinusoids; waveforms use idealized quantities and labeled reference conventions, with exact computations in the lesson formulas.

blocks.title: Combine in quadrature
blocks.strategy: Equate sine and cosine coefficients after expanding R sin(ωt+φ).

blocks.title: Cancellation of anti-phase signals
blocks.strategy: Use the exact identity sin(x+π)=−sin(x) for every real x.
steps: Their sum is zero for every x.
blocks.check: The two equal-amplitude sinusoids are exactly 180° out of phase.

sections.title: Common mistakes, checkpoint, and reference guide

blocks.text: Adding scalar peak amplitudes is generally wrong if the phase differs. The atan(b/a) shortcut loses quadrant information; use atan2(b,a).

blocks.prompt: What is the amplitude of sin x+cos x?
blocks.explanation: The coefficients are a=b=1, so R=√(1²+1²)=√2.

blocks.text: Reference guide (original lessons and questions): Sullivan 9th ed. §4.5; Kelley, Humongous Book of Trigonometry Problems, Chapters 7–8; Lial 10th ed. Chapter 5. Verify wave and phasor sign conventions before applying results.

trig-waves-phase-simple-harmonic-motion.title: Simple harmonic motion
trig-waves-phase-simple-harmonic-motion.summary: Use sinusoidal position, velocity and acceleration to analyze simple harmonic motion and connect amplitude with angular frequency.

blocks.text: In ideal simple harmonic motion (SHM), displacement is x(t)=A cos(ωt+φ), and acceleration is proportional to and opposite displacement: x″=−ω²x. Velocity is the time derivative of position. For constant A and ω, maximum speed is Aω and maximum acceleration magnitude is Aω² (A≥0, ω>0). SI units must be consistent.

blocks.caption: Original schematic for simple harmonic motion; waveforms use idealized quantities and labeled reference conventions, with exact computations in the lesson formulas.

blocks.title: Peak speed in oscillation
blocks.problem: A mass moves as x=0.10cos(20t) m. Find its peak speed.
blocks.strategy: Differentiate and read the magnitude of the sine coefficient.
blocks.check: Aω=0.10×20=2 m/s, consistent with the derivative.

blocks.title: Acceleration at any displacement
blocks.problem: For x=3cos(2t), express acceleration using x.
steps: The angular frequency is ω=2 rad/s.
Thus a=−4x in consistent length/time units.

sections.title: Common mistakes, checkpoint, and reference guide

blocks.text: Amplitude is a position, not a speed; multiply by ω for maximum speed and ω² for maximum acceleration. A physical damped or driven oscillator need not obey the ideal constant-amplitude model.

blocks.prompt: For x=0.2cos(5t) m, what is the maximum speed?
blocks.explanation: The maximum speed is Aω=0.2×5=1 m/s.

blocks.text: Reference guide (original lessons and questions): Sullivan 9th ed. §4.5; Lial 10th ed. §4.5; Young 3rd ed. Chapter 4. Verify wave and phasor sign conventions before applying results.

trig-waves-phase-damped-oscillations.title: Damped oscillations
trig-waves-phase-damped-oscillations.summary: Recognize an exponentially decaying sinusoid, its amplitude envelope, decay rate and time constant without confusing damping with ordinary frequency.

blocks.text: A standard damped-sinusoid model is x(t)=A₀e^(−kt)cos(ω_dt+φ), k>0. The upper and lower envelopes are ±A₀e^(−kt). The amplitude reaches A₀/e after τ=1/k seconds, while the oscillation frequency visible in this model is ω_d/(2π). The damping rate and damped oscillation frequency are different quantities.

blocks.caption: Original schematic for damped oscillations; waveforms use idealized quantities and labeled reference conventions, with exact computations in the lesson formulas.

blocks.title: Time constant
blocks.problem: For x=5e^(−0.25t)cos(8t), determine the amplitude time constant.
blocks.strategy: Compare the exponential factor with e^(−kt).
steps: At t=4 s, the amplitude envelope is 5/e≈1.84.
blocks.check: The ratio of amplitudes at t=4 and t=0 is e^(−1).

blocks.title: Half-amplitude time
blocks.problem: When does an envelope A₀e^(−0.5t) fall to half of A₀?
blocks.strategy: Solve the envelope equation, not the oscillatory cosine.

sections.title: Common mistakes, checkpoint, and reference guide

blocks.text: The exponential envelope is not the instantaneous displacement: the cosine factor changes sign and reaches zero even while the envelope is positive. Distinguish damping k from angular frequency ω_d.

blocks.explanation: Write the exponential as e^(−(1/3)t); the decay rate is 1/3 s⁻¹, so τ=3 s.

blocks.text: Reference guide (original lessons and questions): Sullivan 9th ed. §4.5; Lial 10th ed. §4.5; Young 3rd ed. Chapter 4. Verify wave and phasor sign conventions before applying results.

trig-waves-phase-introductory-ac-wavefor.title: Introductory AC waveforms and phasor connections
trig-waves-phase-introductory-ac-wavefor.summary: Connect sinusoidal voltage and current with peak, RMS, frequency, phase and complex phasor representations using explicit reference conventions.

blocks.text: For a pure sinusoid v(t)=V_m cos(ωt+φ), the RMS voltage is V_m/√2. A phasor is a complex amplitude that preserves magnitude and phase for a fixed frequency. State whether the phasor magnitude is RMS or peak and whether the reference is cosine or sine. Under a cosine-reference RMS convention, v(t)=√2 V_rms cos(ωt+φ) corresponds to V_rms∠φ. Ideal inductive impedance is +jX_L, ideal capacitive impedance is −jX_C.

blocks.caption: Original schematic for introductory ac waveforms and phasor connections; waveforms use idealized quantities and labeled reference conventions, with exact computations in the lesson formulas.

blocks.title: Peak to RMS
blocks.problem: Find RMS voltage for v(t)=10cos(100πt) volts.
blocks.strategy: Apply the sine/cosine RMS relation for a pure sinusoid.
blocks.check: The RMS value is less than the peak, as required.

blocks.title: Cosine-reference phasor
blocks.problem: Convert v(t)=12cos(ωt+30°) V to a peak-magnitude cosine phasor.
steps: Peak magnitude is 12 V and phase is +30°.
The peak phasor is 12∠30° V; the RMS phasor is (12/√2)∠30° V.
blocks.check: Reconstruction with the chosen convention returns 12cos(ωt+30°).

sections.title: Common mistakes, checkpoint, and reference guide

blocks.text: Do not use the same numeric magnitude for peak and RMS phasors. A sine-reference phase is 90° offset from a cosine-reference phase. Lead/lag of ideal L or C follows from voltage = impedance × current, not from a bare sign mnemonic.

blocks.prompt: If a sine wave has 120 V RMS, what is its peak magnitude?
blocks.explanation: For a pure sinusoid V_m=√2 V_rms=120√2 V.

blocks.text: Reference guide (original lessons and questions): Gibilisco, Trigonometry DeMYSTiFieD, Chapter 9; Sullivan 9th ed. §4.5; Lial 10th ed. Chapter 4. Verify wave and phasor sign conventions before applying results.
